title_en: Zhang Dijun v. Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office and Cixi Xinlong Electronics Co., Ltd. — administrative dispute over invalidation of design patent

full_text_en:
Zhang Dijun v. Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office, Cixi Xinlong Electronics Co., Ltd. — administrative dispute over invalidation of design patent

【Ruling Summary】

A product's design typically needs to consider both functional factors and aesthetic factors. The functionality or ornamentality of a product's design features is usually relative. Therefore, there are at least three different types of design features: functional design features, ornamental design features, and design features that are both functional and ornamental.

A functional design feature refers to a design feature that, in the view of the ordinary consumer of the design product, is uniquely determined by the specific function to be achieved, without considering aesthetic factors. The criterion for determining a functional design feature is not whether the design feature lacks selectability due to functional or technical constraints, but whether, in the view of the ordinary consumer, the design feature is determined solely by a specific function, such that it is unnecessary to consider whether the design feature has aesthetic appeal. Functional design features generally do not have a significant impact on the overall visual effect of the design.

Supreme People's Court Administrative Judgment

(2012) Xing Ti Zi No. 14

Applicant for Retrial (Defendant at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance): Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office. Domicile: Floors 10-12, Yin'gu Building, No. 9, West Road North Fourth Ring, Haidian District, Beijing.

Legal Representative: Zhang Maoyu, Deputy Director of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Qian Yijun, Examiner of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Mao Jin, Examiner of the Board.

Respondent (Plaintiff at First Instance, Appellee at Second Instance): Zhang Dijun, male, Han Chinese, born on September 25, 1967, residing at Lujia Road, Changfeng Village, Changhe Town, Cixi City, Zhejiang Province.

Agent ad litem: Wang Weidong, male, Han Chinese, born on October 29, 1969, residing at Room 502, Unit 2, Building 833, Jinbu Street, Daowai District, Harbin City, Heilongjiang Province, staff member of Beijing Jiecheng Xintong Intellectual Property Agency Co., Ltd.

Third Party at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance: Cixi Xinlong Electronics Co., Ltd. Domicile: Dalutou Industrial Zone, Changhe Town, Cixi City, Zhejiang Province.

Legal Representative: Tong Xinxiang, Manager of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Ge Hongbin, Lawyer of Zhejiang Weizhi Law Firm.

Applicant for Retrial: Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office (hereinafter referred to as the Patent Reexamination Board) in the administrative dispute over invalidation of design patent with Respondent Zhang Dijun and Third Party at First Instance Cixi Xinlong Electronics Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Xinlong Company). The Patent Reexamination Board, dissatisfied with the Administrative Judgment (2010) Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 1459 rendered by the Beijing High People's Court on March 17, 2011, applied to this Court for retrial. This Court rendered the Administrative Ruling (2011) Zhi Xing Zi No. 81 on November 29, 2011, deciding to bring the case for retrial. This Court formed a collegial panel according to law and held a public hearing on March 27, 2012. Agents ad litem of the Applicant for Retrial the Patent Reexamination Board, Qian Yijun and Mao Jin, the Agent ad litem of the Respondent Zhang Dijun, Wang Weidong, and the Agent ad litem of the Third Party at First Instance Xinlong Company, Ge Hongbin, appeared in court to participate in the proceedings. The trial of this case has now concluded.

Zhang Dijun, dissatisfied with the Decision No. 13912 on Examination of Request for Patent Invalidation (hereinafter referred to as Decision No. 13912) rendered by the Patent Reexamination Board on September 15, 2009, filed an administrative lawsuit with the Beijing First Intermediate People's Court on December 21, 2009. Zhang Dijun alleged that he was the patentee of the design patent titled "Logic Programming Switch (SR14)" (hereinafter referred to as this patent), and that Decision No. 13912 of the Patent Reexamination Board declaring this patent invalid was erroneous. This patent and the prior design were neither identical nor similar. This patent is a design of a logic programming switch, while the prior design is a design of a rotary switch for household appliances. For these two types of products, the number and positional distribution of pins directly affect whether the product can be adapted to the PCB board of the corresponding electronic product, and thus differences in the number and positional distribution of pins have a significant impact on the overall visual effect of such products. Although both this patent and the prior design have five pins, the pins of this patent are all arranged on one side of the base, while in the prior design only three pins are arranged on one side of the base and the other two pins are arranged on the opposite side. An ordinary consumer would notice the difference in the positional distribution of pins and would not be confused or misled.

The Patent Reexamination Board argued that this patent and the prior design were similar designs, that Decision No. 13912 had clearly ascertained facts, correctly applied law, and followed lawful procedures, and that the plaintiff's grounds of action were untenable. It requested that Decision No. 13912 be upheld.

Xinlong Company submitted its opinion stating that design features mainly determined by technical functions and features such as materials and internal structures that do not affect the overall visual effect should not be considered as factors in determining whether the overall visual effects are similar. Decision No. 13912 was correct, and it requested that the decision be upheld and the plaintiff's claims be dismissed.

The Beijing First Intermediate People's Court found upon trial that this patent was a design titled "Logic Programming Switch (SR14)" with patent number 200630128900.0, filed on August 4, 2006, and granted and published on June 7, 2007. The patentee was Zhang Dijun. The six views published for this patent included: front view, left and right views, top and bottom views, and rear view. Its upper portion had a basic shape of a roughly stepped cylinder that was thinner at the top and thicker at the bottom, with one side of the thin cylinder cut off. The lower portion was a roughly flat rectangular prism, with two pairs of opposite sides each having two clamping legs, and on the other pair of opposite sides, one side had five pins and the other side had no pins.

On May 31, 2009, Xinlong Company filed a request for invalidation with the Patent Reexamination Board on the ground that this patent did not comply with Article 23 of the Patent Law revised in 2000 (hereinafter referred to as the Patent Law), and submitted 9 pieces of evidence. Among them, Evidence 7 was Chinese Design Patent No. 00302321.4, with a grant and publication date of October 25, 2000. Exhibit 7 disclosed a design of a rotary switch, with an upper portion having a basic shape of a roughly stepped cylinder that was thinner at the top and thicker at the bottom, with one side of the thin cylinder cut off, and a rectangular groove on one side of the thick cylinder. The lower portion was a roughly flat rectangular prism, with two pairs of opposite sides each having two clamping legs, and on the other pair of opposite sides, there were three pins and two pins respectively (i.e., the prior design).

On September 2, 2009, the Patent Reexamination Board conducted an oral hearing on Xinlong Company's invalidation request. During the oral hearing, Zhang Dijun acknowledged the authenticity of Exhibit 7. The Patent Reexamination Board found upon examination that this patent and the prior design were both designs of switches with the same use, belonging to the same category of products, and thus comparable. The main differences were: the prior design had an additional rectangular groove on the upper thick cylinder, and the positions of the pins on the lower portion were different. Since the simplified groove design in this patent compared to the prior design was only a local minor change relative to the overall shape, and the difference in pin positions was a local positional variation dictated by the connection function, neither had a significant impact on the overall design of the two products. At the same time, other more minor differences were also clearly insufficient to have a significant impact on the overall visual effect. The specific designs of the main shapes and their combinations were the same or similar, constituting similar designs. Since a similar design had been publicly published in a publication before the filing date of this patent, this patent did not comply with Article 23 of the Patent Law. On September 15, 2009, the Patent Reexamination Board rendered Decision No. 13912 declaring this patent completely invalid.

During the first instance trial, Zhang Dijun acknowledged the facts found by the Patent Reexamination Board that the upper thick cylinder of the prior design had a rectangular groove while this patent did not, and that the pin positions on the lower portion were different. He also stated that although both this patent and the prior design had five pins, all five pins of this patent were arranged on one side of the base, while in the prior design only three pins were arranged on one side of the base and the other two pins were arranged on the opposite side. The Patent Reexamination Board acknowledged the other differences raised by Zhang Dijun, but considered these differences to be minor, and that the difference in pins was determined by function. In the absence of evidence submitted by Zhang Dijun, this could not be considered from the perspective of design space.

The first instance court held that in determining whether designs are identical or similar, the judgment subject in the relevant field plays an important role in the objective determination of the conclusion. Both this patent and the prior design are components of electrical equipment, and the relevant consumers should be professionals engaged in the production and procurement of electrical products. Comparing this patent and the prior design, the prior design had a rectangular groove on the upper thick cylinder while this patent did not; the pin positions on the lower portion were different: all five pins of this patent were on one side of the base, while in the prior design only three pins were on one side and the other two were on the opposite side. Relevant consumers in this field, when selecting such products, will pay greater attention to these parts of the product. Therefore, the differences in these parts had a significant impact on the overall visual effect and would not cause confusion or mistaken recognition between the two. Decision No. 13912 was insufficient in main evidence and should be revoked according to law. The Beijing First Intermediate People's Court, in accordance with Article 54(2)(1) of the Administrative Procedure Law, rendered Administrative Judgment (2010) Yi Zhong Zhi Xing Chu Zi No. 533: 1. Revoked Decision No. 13912 on Examination of Request for Invalidation rendered by the Patent Reexamination Board on December 21, 2009; 2. The Patent Reexamination Board shall re-render a decision on the invalidation request filed by Xinlong Company against the design patent titled "Logic Programming Switch (SR14)". The case acceptance fee of RMB 100 shall be borne by the Patent Reexamination Board.

Both the Patent Reexamination Board and Xinlong Company were dissatisfied with the first instance judgment and appealed to the Beijing High People's Court. The Patent Reexamination Board requested the revocation of the first instance judgment and the upholding of Decision No. 13912. Its main grounds of appeal were: the first instance judgment erred in its determination of the judgment subject and the differences between this patent and the prior design; the difference in pins between this patent and the prior design was a local positional variation dictated by the connection function. Xinlong Company requested the revocation of the first instance judgment and the amendment to dismiss all of Zhang Dijun's claims. Its main grounds of appeal were: the differences between this patent and the prior design were minor; the difference in pins was a technical arrangement, easily causing confusion among ordinary consumers, and this patent and the prior design already constituted similar designs.

The second instance court found upon trial that the facts found at first instance were true.

The Beijing High People's Court held at second instance that in determining whether designs are similar, the judgment subject must first be determined. Different judgment subjects, due to differences in their knowledge level and cognitive ability regarding the compared design product, may reach different conclusions when determining whether two designs are similar. According to the Patent Examination Guidelines, in determining whether designs are similar, evaluation should be based on the knowledge level and cognitive ability of the ordinary consumer of the compared design product. The so-called "ordinary consumer" is specific; different categories of compared design products have different consumer groups. In this case, the publication date of the prior design was earlier than the filing date of this patent, and the two belong to the same category of products, so the prior design can be used to evaluate whether this patent complies with Article 23 of the Patent Law. Both this patent and the prior design are components of electrical equipment; the production and procurement personnel of relevant products have a certain cognitive ability regarding such electronic components and objectively are familiar with the appearance and functions of such products. Therefore, the first instance court's determination that such personnel are the "ordinary consumers" of this category of product was not erroneous. The Patent Reexamination Board's ground of appeal that the first instance court erred in determining the judgment subject as the "ordinary consumer" cannot be sustained and is not supported. Comparing this patent with the prior design, the prior design had a rectangular groove on the upper thick cylinder while this patent did not; all five pins of this patent were arranged on one side of the base, while in the prior design only three pins were arranged on one side and the other two pins were arranged on the opposite side. In the view of ordinary consumers, the above differences between this patent and the prior design could have a significant impact on the overall visual effect of the two. Ordinary consumers, when selecting such products, will also pay greater attention to these parts of the product and will generally not be confused or mistaken between the two. The first instance court's determination that the two do not constitute identical or similar designs was not erroneous. The grounds of appeal of the Patent Reexamination Board and Xinlong Company cannot be sustained, and their appeal requests are not supported. The first instance judgment found facts basically clearly and applied the law correctly, and should be upheld according to law. In accordance with Article 61(1) of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the Beijing High People's Court rendered Administrative Judgment (2010) Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 1459 on March 17, 2011: appeal dismissed, and the original judgment affirmed. The first instance case acceptance fee of RMB 100 shall be borne by the Patent Reexamination Board; the second instance case acceptance fee of RMB 100 shall be borne half each by the Patent Reexamination Board and Xinlong Company.

The Patent Reexamination Board applied to this Court for retrial, alleging that the second instance judgment adopted an improper method for determining whether this patent and the prior design were identical or similar, and reached an erroneous conclusion. This patent and the prior design should be considered similar designs. It requested the revocation of the second instance judgment and the upholding of Decision No. 13912. Its main reasons were:

1. The second instance judgment erred in its application of the judgment method. The second instance judgment did not reach its conclusion based on the method of overall observation and comprehensive assessment, but only observed the visual effects brought by the differences on the overall appearance, while ignoring the impact of the similarities on the overall visual effect.

2. The "ordinary consumer" of this patented product should be the purchasers and users of electronic components, who should understand the functions and use environments of each part of such products, and be able to distinguish which designs are specific shapes dictated by function. Compared with conventional designs, only variable content and design content that has a significant impact on the overall visual effect are of concern to ordinary consumers. From the perspective of ordinary consumers, the differences between this patent and the prior design are all functional and technical, and do not have a significant impact on the overall visual effect. The overall visual effects of the two are similar.

(1) The differences between this patent and the prior technology are technical. Generally speaking, when a difference is designed based on technical requirements regarding product function, performance, economy, convenience, safety, etc., that difference should be considered functional. When a difference is designed to make the product visually beautiful, distinctive, or eye-catching, that difference should be considered ornamental. The pins of both this patent and the prior design are inserted into the circuit board to connect with other electronic components. The different pin arrangements are based on different circuit layout needs on the circuit board and also based on requirements for product function and convenience. This patent does not have the notch on the middle annular shaft of the prior design; it is a single-shaft structure, and only the upper cylindrical shaft with a notch can rotate to adjust signal output. The prior design, however, is a dual-shaft structure, where both the upper and middle shafts can rotate for signal output. The only difference is in the signal control method: this patent can only control pulse phase through the upper shaft, while the prior design can both control pulse phase through the upper shaft and adjust pulse amplitude through the middle shaft. This is designed based on different needs for product function and performance.

(2) The effects achieved by the differences between this patent and the prior design are objective. The effects achieved by technical features are technical in nature and can be verified or predicted through objective means such as experiments and reasoning. The effects achieved by ornamental features are aesthetic, and different subjects obtain different subjective feelings due to different aesthetic orientations, social culture, and other factors. The effect achieved by the different pin arrangement in this patent and the prior design is to provide circuit layouts for different circuits, meeting the standardized application of electronic accessories. The presence or absence of a notch on the middle annular shaft serves to achieve different signal control functions. The effects achieved by the above differences are all objective and are not affected by the subject's aesthetic orientation or sociocultural feelings.

(3) From the perspective of selectability of design features, the selectability of this patent and the prior design is limited by function or technology. Ornamental features are not constrained by function or technology and, due to the uncertainty of aesthetics, are selectable. Functional designs, on the other hand, are limited by product function or technical conditions and are either not selectable or their selectability is limited by functional requirements or technical specifications. As standardized electronic accessories, the pin arrangement of this patent and the prior design is dictated by technical specifications. The groove on the middle annular post is for engaging with the driving device of the switch, and the shape and size of the groove are also dictated by technical specifications.

3. The subject matter protected by design patents is ornamental (i.e., aesthetic) designs, excluding the protection of functional or technical features. For electronic components and other parts that are not visible in the final use of the product, the shape design is based on considerations of fit and coordination, not aesthetic considerations, and thus should not be protected by design patents. If a functional design that does not meet the patentability standards for invention or utility model patents obtains design patent protection, the patentee essentially achieves a monopoly over a non-innovative functional shape through the design patent system, deviating from the legislative purpose of patent protection.

Zhang Dijun submitted his opinion, stating that the second instance judgment's method was correct and its determination of the knowledge level of ordinary consumers was correct. The Patent Reexamination Board's assertion that the differences between this patent and the prior technology were functional or technical lacked a basis. The design space for this patented product was very small. In the prior art, pins were always arranged on opposite sides of the base, whereas this patent arranged all pins on one side of the base, which played a role in significantly changing the overall visual effect of the product. As for the groove on the middle annular post, some products have it and some do not, indicating that the groove is not uniquely determined by the product's function and cannot be regarded as determined by product function. Since the groove in the prior design occupied about three-quarters of the middle annular post, the absence of a groove on the middle annular post of this patent cannot be considered a minor change.

Xinlong Company submitted its opinion, stating that it agreed with the retrial request and reasons of the Patent Reexamination Board. The second instance judgment erred both in finding facts and applying law. The differences between this patent and the prior technology were local minor differences and were clearly functional designs.

This Court finds upon trial that the facts found by the lower courts are true.

During the retrial, the Patent Reexamination Board submitted the product sample catalogue "2006 Switches/Encoders" of Japan's ALPS Corporation, which had been submitted by Xinlong Company during the patent invalidation proceedings, as well as the claims, specification, and drawings of a Chinese utility model patent titled "A Dual-Axis Encoder," Patent No. 200920220081.0, for the court's reference but not as evidence in this case. The Patent Reexamination Board argued that, with reference to the above documents, it can be seen that the product involved in the prior design is a dual-axis rotatable logic programming switch, and the function of the rectangular groove on its upper thick column is to facilitate connection with external electrical appliances. The lower right corner of the back cover of the product sample catalogue "2006 Switches/Encoders" of Japan's ALPS Corporation indicates that the printing time was January 2006. Pages 171 to 235 of the catalogue contain images of various types of encoders, among which many encoders have no rectangular groove on the upper thick column, and a few encoders have a rectangular groove on the upper thick column. Zhang Dijun challenged the source, authenticity, and publication time of the product sample catalogue "2006 Switches/Encoders" of Japan's ALPS Corporation. The filing date of the Chinese utility model patent titled "A Dual-Axis Encoder" was October 23, 2009, and its authorization announcement date was August 4, 2010. Claim 6 of its claims states: "The dual-axis encoder according to claim 1, characterized in that: the tail end of the outer shaft core (2) is provided with a groove (21) to facilitate connection and installation with an external electrical appliance." Zhang Dijun argued that the filing date of the above patent is later than the filing date of the patent in question, and the patent document of the prior design itself does not describe the function of the groove; therefore, the existing evidence in this case cannot prove the role and function of the groove in the prior design.

During the retrial hearing, the Patent Reexamination Board, Zhang Dijun, and Xinlong Company all recognized that the patent in question is an encoding switch that achieves encoding output through rotation, used in situations requiring output signal adjustment such as in rice cookers and electric ovens. In use, the end of the encoding switch is fitted with a knob that engages with it; the number of pins of the encoding switch is specific, and their distribution needs to match the circuit board nodes.

This court holds that, since the filing date of the patent in question is before October 1, 2009, the provisions of the Patent Law of the People's Republic of China as revised in 2000 and its implementing regulations should apply. In light of the retrial applicant's retrial application, the appellee's defense, and the trial circumstances, the focus of the dispute in this case is: whether the original second-instance judgment violated the judgment method of overall observation and comprehensive assessment; whether technical design features and decorative design features are separable and their criteria and roles for distinction; whether the distinguishing design features between the patent in question and the prior design are functional design features; and whether the patent in question is identical or similar to the prior design.

(I) Whether the original second-instance judgment violated the judgment method of overall observation and comprehensive assessment

The so-called method of overall observation and comprehensive assessment means that, when determining whether a design patent is identical or similar to a prior design, one should proceed from the knowledge level and cognitive ability of the ordinary consumer of the design patent product, comprehensively assess the impact of the similarities and differences between the two on the overall visual effect, and make a judgment on whether the overall visual effects of the two are identical or similar. In this process, attention must be paid to the impact of both the similarities and the differences on the overall visual effect. In fact, as long as the determination of whether the design patent and the prior design are identical or similar is based on the identity or similarity of their overall visual images, a comprehensive consideration of the degree of influence of the similarities and differences on the overall visual image is necessarily required. In this case, based on the comparison between the patent in question and the prior design, the original second-instance judgment identified two design differences between the two and further held that the above differences could significantly impact the overall visual effect of the two. It can be seen that, although the original second-instance judgment focused on the impact of the differences on the overall visual effect, it did not overlook the impact of the similarities on the overall visual effect. The Patent Reexamination Board contends that the original second-instance judgment only observed the visual effect brought by the differences to the whole but turned a blind eye to the impact of the similarities on the overall visual effect. This contention cannot be established, and this court does not support it.

(II) Whether technical design features and decorative design features are separable and their criteria and roles for distinction

The Patent Reexamination Board believes that design features can be divided into functional features and decorative features. Functional features are designed based on technical requirements regarding product function, performance, economy, convenience, safety, etc.; decorative features are designed based on the visual aesthetic effect of the product. The effect achieved by functional features is objective and not influenced by the subject's aesthetic orientation or socio-cultural feelings; the effect achieved by decorative features is aesthetic, and different subjects may have different subjective feelings due to different aesthetic orientations, socio-cultural factors, etc. Functional features are limited by product function or technical conditions and lack selectivity, or their selectivity is restricted by functional requirements or technical specifications; decorative features are not constrained by function or technology and have selectivity due to aesthetic uncertainty. This involves the issues of whether functional design features and decorative design features are separable and their criteria and significance for distinction. This court comments as follows:

First, regarding the distinction between functional design features and decorative design features. The appearance design of any product usually needs to consider two basic elements: functional factors and aesthetic factors. That is, the product must first fulfill its function, and second, it must be visually aesthetic. It can be said that most products are a combination of functionality and decoration. For a specific design feature of a certain design product, the dual needs of function and aesthetics also need to be considered; it is the result of a compromise and balance between technicality and decoration. Therefore, the functionality or decorativeness of a product's design features is usually relative, and it is unrealistic to absolutely distinguish between functional design features and decorative design features in most cases. Only in special circumstances can a certain design feature of a certain product be completely determined by decoration or function. Therefore, there are at least three different types of design features: functional design features, decorative design features, and design features that are both functional and decorative.

Second, regarding the criteria for distinguishing functional design features. Functional design features refer to those design features that, from the perspective of the ordinary consumer of the design patent product, are uniquely determined by the specific function to be achieved and do not consider aesthetic factors. There is a certain correlation between functional design features and the selectivity of such design features. If a certain design feature is the only design determined by a specific function, then there is no room for considering aesthetic factors in such a design feature, and it clearly falls within the category of functional design features. If a certain design feature is one of a limited number of design methods to achieve a specific function, this fact is strong evidence that the design feature is a functional feature. However, even if a certain design feature is only one of many design methods to achieve a specific function, as long as the design feature is solely determined by the specific function to be achieved and has no relation to aesthetic considerations, it can still be determined as a functional design feature. If functional design features are merely understood as the only design to achieve a certain function, it would overly limit the scope of functional design features, excluding design features with two or more alternative designs, and thereby allowing design patent applicants to monopolize specific functions by filing design patent applications for limited alternative designs, which is inconsistent with the legislative purpose of design patent protection for innovative designs with aesthetic appeal. From this perspective, the criterion for determining a functional design feature is not whether the design feature lacks selectivity due to functional or technical constraints, but whether, from the perspective of the ordinary consumer, the design feature is solely determined by a specific function, without needing to consider whether the design feature has aesthetic appeal.

Finally, regarding the significance of distinguishing different types of design features. Different types of design features have different impacts on the overall visual effect of the design product. Functional design features typically do not have a significant impact on the overall visual effect of the design; decorative features generally have an impact on the overall visual effect of the design; for design features that are both functional and decorative, the impact on the overall visual effect depends on the strength of their decorative nature; the stronger the decorative nature, the relatively greater the impact on the overall visual effect may be, and vice versa. Of course, the above are only general principles. The impact of a design feature on the overall visual effect of a design product ultimately needs to be comprehensively assessed based on the specific circumstances of the case.

(III) Whether the distinguishing design features between the patent in question and the prior design are functional design features

Both Decision No. 13912 and the original first and second-instance judgments determined that, compared with the prior design, the patent in question has two differences: the prior design's upper thick column has a rectangular groove, while the patent in question does not (Difference Feature 1); the pin positions at the lower part are different, with all five pins of the patent in question on one side of the base, while in the prior design, only three pins are on one side of the base, and the other two pins are on the opposite side (Difference Feature 2). The parties in this case have no objection to the above differences, and this court confirms them.

Regarding Difference Feature 1: The upper thick column of the patent in question has no rectangular groove, while the prior design's upper thick column has a rectangular groove. First, because the patent document of the prior design itself does not provide any explanation as to whether the patented product is a single-axis or dual-axis structure, whether it can rotate on two axes, or what function the rectangular groove performs, it is difficult to determine the structure of the prior design product and the function of the rectangular groove under these circumstances. Second, Decision No. 13912 itself did not determine that the rectangular groove on the upper thick column of the prior design is a functional design; the Patent Reexamination Board only raised the argument that the rectangular groove is a functional design during the retrial application stage. In this regard, the Patent Reexamination Board should provide sufficient evidence to prove it. Finally, the filing date of the Chinese utility model patent titled "A Dual-Axis Encoder," which the Patent Reexamination Board submitted to this court for reference, is later than the filing date of the patent in question, and the function of the groove on the outer shaft core as described in its claim 6 is to facilitate connection and installation with an external electrical appliance, which is not entirely consistent with the Patent Reexamination Board's argument. It is difficult to determine the function of the rectangular groove on the upper thick column of the prior design based on this. Therefore, based on the existing evidence in this case, it cannot be determined that the prior design product is a dual-axis rotatable programming switch, nor can it be determined that its rectangular groove is used to cooperate with a knob to achieve adjustment of signal output. The Patent Reexamination Board's argument that the notch on the middle annular shaft in the prior design is for achieving different signal control functions and that Difference Feature 1 is a functional design feature lacks sufficient basis, and this court does not support it.

Regarding Difference Feature 2: The pin positions at the lower part of the patent in question and the prior design are different. All parties in this case confirm that the number of pins of the encoding switch involved in the patent in question is specific, and their distribution needs to match the circuit board nodes. It can be seen that the number and position distribution of the pins are determined by the circuit board that cooperates with them, so as to match the nodes on different circuit boards. From the perspective of the ordinary consumer of the product of the patent in question, whether the pins are distributed on one side of the base or on two opposite sides is based on the needs of the circuit board layout that cooperates with them, in order to achieve adaptation and connection between the two, without involving consideration of aesthetic factors. Therefore, Difference Feature 2 is a functional design feature and does not have a significant impact on the overall visual effect of the product of the patent in question. The Patent Reexamination Board's retrial reason that Difference Feature 2 is a functional design feature is established, and this court supports it.

(IV) Whether the patent in question and the prior design are identical or similar

As previously mentioned, compared with the prior design, the patent in question has two distinguishing features. Among them, Difference Feature 2 is a functional design feature and does not have a significant impact on the overall visual effect of the patent in question and the prior design. With respect to Difference Feature 1, the existing evidence cannot sufficiently prove that the rectangular groove on the upper thick column of the prior design is a functional design feature. At the same time, the rectangular groove is relatively obvious and is not a subtle change compared to the overall design. Nevertheless, in light of the facts found by this court, the absence of a rectangular groove on the upper thick column of the encoding switch is a common and ordinary design. The encoder images on pages 171 to 194 of the product sample catalogue "2006 Switches/Encoders" of Japan's ALPS Corporation also support this point as auxiliary evidence. As a common and ordinary design, the absence of a rectangular groove on the upper thick column of the patent in question does not have a significant impact on the overall visual effect and is insufficient to cause a clear difference in the overall visual effect between the patent in question and the prior design. Since neither of the two distinguishing design features has a significant impact on the overall visual effect of the patent in question, the similarities between the patent in question and the prior design have a greater impact on the overall visual effect, and the two constitute similar designs. The original first and second-instance judgments, which held that the two do not constitute identical or similar designs, erred in the application of law and should be corrected. The corresponding retrial reason of the Patent Reexamination Board is established and should be supported. Although the determination of fact by the Patent Reexamination Board in Decision No. 13912 that Difference Feature 1 between the patent in question and the prior design is a local subtle change relative to the overall shape is somewhat improper, the conclusion that the patent in question and the prior design constitute similar designs is correct and should be upheld.

In summary, the original first and second-instance judgments, which held that the patent in question and the prior design are neither identical nor similar, erred in the application of law and should be revoked according to law. Decision No. 13912 of the Patent Reexamination Board correctly applied laws and regulations and had a lawful procedure, and should be upheld. Pursuant to Article 23 of the Patent Law of the People's Republic of China as revised in 2000, Article 54(1) and Article 63(2) of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 76(1) and Article 78 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the judgment is as follows:

1. Revoke the Administrative Judgment (2010) Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 1459 of the Beijing High People's Court and the Administrative Judgment (2010) Yi Zhong Zhi Xing Chu Zi No. 533 of the Beijing First Intermediate People's Court;

2. Uphold the Review Decision on Invalidation Declaration Request No. 13912 of the Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office.

The first-instance case acceptance fee and the second-instance case acceptance fee, each 100 yuan, shall be borne by Zhang Dijun.

This judgment is final.
